analysis.one_liner: Ends every federal tax under the tax code after 2001, naming no replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 93 cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut off every tax collected under the federal tax code — income tax, estate and gift taxes, excise taxes, and the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare — after December 31, 2001. It did not create a replacement system. Instead, it stated that whatever Congress builds next should be simple, low-rate, and protective of Social Security and Medicare, and it said Congress would need a supermajority to raise taxes under the new system.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed as written, the biggest winners would be high-income households and large estates, since the code it terminates includes the progressive income tax and the estate tax. Everyone would stop paying taxes temporarily, but the bill provides no substitute funding for any federal program.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any tax under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2001, ending income, estate and gift, and excise taxation [S2, S3].

It declares that a replacement system should apply a low rate to all Americans, provide tax relief for working Americans, eliminate the bias against savings and investment, and not penalize marriage or families [S3].
It would require a supermajority of both houses of Congress for any new system to raise taxes, and declares the new system should protect the integrity of Social Security and Medicare [S3].

The bill's subjects include estate tax, income tax, inheritance tax, Medicare, and old-age, survivors, and disability insurance, indicating the payroll taxes financing those programs were within its reach [S1].

analysis.who_pays: As written, the bill cuts off all funding raised under the tax code — roughly the entire federal budget — with no replacement, threatening Social Security and Medicare checks, federal salaries, and every program funded through the code, unless Congress enacted a new tax system before the deadline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal funding

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the tax code without enacting a replacement, so unless Congress passed an entirely new tax system by the end of 2001, the federal government would lose the revenue it uses to pay for Social Security, Medicare, defense, and everything else [S2, S3].

The bill's own text requires the new system to protect Social Security and Medicare, but the payroll taxes that fund those programs are part of the code being terminated, and the bill contains no transition plan to bridge the gap [S3].
Requiring a supermajority of both houses to raise taxes under any successor system would make future revenue adjustments much harder, shifting power toward any minority bloc in either chamber [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As a statement of principles — simpler taxes, lower rates, an end to the code — the bill communicates a clear position. As law, it would have been badly designed: it eliminates all federal revenue on a fixed date without a replacement, transition funding, or a mechanism for writing the new system, which is why bills of this shape function mainly as political declarations rather than workable legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Largent introduced the bill on September 17, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5, S1].
Ninety-three members cosponsored it — 90 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill expired with the end of the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999 [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost materially — the bill never advanced, so the existing tax system and the programs it funds continued unchanged. Had it somehow passed as written, high-income households would have gained the most and every federal program would have faced a funding cliff.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax system stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Steve Largent
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Internal Revenue Code after 2001.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or vote after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The 93 cosponsors were 90 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and the bill received no action in the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee [S4, S5].

industries.note: Terminating the code ends the progressive income tax and the estate and gift taxes, the taxes that fall most heavily on top earners and large inheritances, and the bill names no replacement revenue. The cost of that gain would fall on every federal program, including Social Security and Medicare.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Ending the income tax would eliminate the compliance work — filing, audits, record-keeping — that this industry is built on. Any benefit to ordinary filers would depend entirely on whatever replacement system Congress enacted, which the bill does not specify.
